newsitem.title: JAPAN: E.Asian Grains - Trade stuck in Christmas slumber.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grains - Trade stuck in Christmas slumber.

text.p: The grains and oilseeds business from Japan to the Philippines will probably slip into a coma this week as people take off for a long Christmas holiday, regional traders said on Monday.

Only a sharp drop in grains and oilseeds futures prices in the United States could induce some buyers to wake up and come in for some bargain-hunting, although the prospect looked dim, the traders said.
"If there's major price fluctuations, we may return to the market. But we're going to keep a low profile this week," a major trade house official in Tokyo said.

"We expect Korean buyers to hold back their grain purchases until USDA (U.S. Department of Agriculture) releases the January (crop) report," a trader with Cheiljedang Corp in South Korea said. The USDA will release the report on January 9.
Japanese premiums for U.S. soybeans were quoted at about 130 U.S. cents a bushel over the Chicago Board of Trade's (CBOT) March contract.
Local trade houses in Japan are negotiating with Argentina on possible corn import contracts for 1997 and details will be made clear early next month.
Japan's Food Agency is to carry out an import tender for 7,000 tonnes of rice on December 25. An agency official said one more import tender next week is under consideration.
In South Korea, traders expect buyers to purchase about 20,000 to 30,000 tonnes of soymeal by the end of this month.
Korean and Taiwanese buyers were also monitoring the offer prices of Chinese corn after reports resurfaced among regional dealers that Beijing may allow corn exports in the first quarter of 1997.
"If Chinese corn prices are quoted lower than the U.S. corn, we will buy the Chinese one," an official with the National Livestock Cooperatives Federation (NLCF).
The NLCF offcial said Chinese corn was hovering at around US$135 per tonne FOB if shipped from a nearby port in China. But prices of Chinese corn, however, remain high, the official added.
Taiwanese dealers said that Chinese corn is at least $10 tonne more expensive than U.S. corn.
Taiwanese traders said the bumper Chinese corn crop may also not reach the market any time soon.
"China's export clearance process is sometimes very slow and there are other uncertainties," a corn trader in Taipei said. "China's government could block a corn export at any time."

China's corn output is expected to reach 118.5 million tonnes this year, up from 106 million tonnes in 1995, according to the China Grain, Oils and Feeds newsletter. The publication forecast output for 1997 to reach 122.5 million tonnes.
The subdued situation in the market was likewise mirrored in the Philippines and Taiwan.
"Taiwan buyers will remain sidelined until mid-January," a trader in Taipei said.

Taiwan's Hui Shung Group was planning to place a tender for combined cargo of 54,000 tonnes of U.S. corn and soybeans, but reset the tender to January due to high freight prices, a Hui Shung official said.
The freight cost from the Pacific Northwest was seen at about $13.50 per tonne and Gulf of Mexico ranged between $23.50 and $24.50 per tonne, both for Panamax-sized March shipments.
The NLCF official in Korea quoted the freight rate from the U.S. Pacific Northwest at $14.00 to $14.50 per tonne and the rate from the U.S. Gulf was seen at $24.00 to $24.50 a tonne.
Freight from the U.S. Gulf was seen at about $19 a tonne a few months ago.
Grain prices in Taiwan climbed recently as the market reacted to shipment delays caused by a tanker crashing into an embankment on the Mississippi river in New Orleans.

The ship was supposed to deliver three shipments totalling 144,000 tonnes of corn and 16,000 tonnes of soybeans to Taiwan. The Philippines will also shy away from the market because of ample supplies, traders said.
"I expect the wheat orders for January shipments to stop" this week, one trader said.
